question.text: Will James Comey have at least two federal criminal cases pending against him on November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question is resolved by the status, as of 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026, of federal district-court criminal dockets naming James Comey as a defendant — principally United States v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM (D.D.C.) and United States v. Comey, No. 4:26-cr-00016-FL-RN (E.D.N.C.) — as shown in public court records (PACER/CourtListener) or, where those records cannot be accessed, [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions). A federal criminal case counts as pending if a charging document (indictment, superseding indictment, or information) naming Comey as a defendant is on file and the case has not been finally disposed of by a judgment. A case remains pending unless every charging document in it has been dismissed in full; dismissal of only some counts, or a superseding indictment filed under the same case number, leaves it one pending case, and a dismissal order takes effect on its entry even if stayed or later appealed. The question resolves Yes if at least two such cases are pending on that date, counting any federal district-court criminal case against him that is pending then regardless of when it was filed, including a previously dismissed case that has been reinstated or re-charged; it resolves No if one or zero are pending. Proceedings in a U.S. Court of Appeals (including Nos. 25-4673 and 25-4674) are not pending criminal cases for purposes of this question.
question.fine_print: A charging document filed under seal counts as pending provided a corresponding entry appears on the case docket.

research:
I found nothing from November 1 to 3, 2026 showing that either pending case has been dismissed, or that a D.C. grand jury has returned an indictment or a no-bill. The deciding events are still ahead: the reported November 5 deadline in D.C. and a possible ruling by Judge Flanagan in E.D.N.C.

## 1. Resolution source
- The deciding records are the PACER/CourtListener dockets for No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM (D.D.C.) and No. 4:26-cr-00016-FL-RN (E.D.N.C.). CourtListener refused my request (HTTP 403), so I could not read either docket directly. Everything below comes from news coverage.
- 2026-10-30: The D.D.C. case was still pending. McFadden "took under advisement" Comey's motion to dismiss the October 5 information and left the government free to pursue an indictment. [ksl](https://www.ksl.com/article/51642507/judge-puts-off-decision-in-comey-case-as-prosecutors-pursue-new-indictment)
- 2026-10-09 (latest substantive coverage I found): E.D.N.C. motions were ripe and Flanagan had set no oral argument. She may rule on the briefs. [gvwire](https://gvwire.com/2026/10/09/the-seashells-case-against-comey-at-a-crossroads/)

## 2. Current status
- Nothing settles the question yet. Searches through November 3 found no dismissal in either case, no D.C. indictment and no no-bill.
- 2026-11-02: Coverage still lists the seashell case as pending. CNN said earlier that Comey "still faces" the North Carolina charges. [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/26/politics/james-comey-charged)

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: In a related matter, Magistrate Judge Faruqui dismissed the DOJ case against former FBI officials Floris and Benavides for lack of probable cause, calling it "weaponization." That case was filed October 20, 2026. [HNGN](https://www.hngn.com/articles/273674/20261102/judge-calls-doj-case-against-ex-fbi-officials-weaponization-tosses-it.htm)
- 2026-10-30, D.D.C. hearing:
  - McFadden said it was unclear whether he would rule by "next Thursday" (November 5). ABC called that "technically the last day for the government to seek a grand jury indictment" before the information is dismissed under the Speedy Trial Act. [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147)
  - CBS adds a detail I could not reconcile: after an earlier emergency hearing, DOJ "agreed not to seek an indictment for 30 days." [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/)
  - DOJ lawyer Dustin Farahnak said the department is "still going to the grand jury very diligently." He cited new evidence of overt acts as late as April 2017, which could extend the charging window by about six months. [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/30/politics/comey-motion-hearing-leak-charges)
  - McFadden remarked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days" and warned against any "dawn raid." [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/james-comey-team-court-seeking-toss-third-doj-case-longtime-trump-foe-rcna606394)
- 2026-10-26: The D.C. information was unsealed. It was filed October 5, the last day before the ten-year limit ran out. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/26/james-comey-indictment-national-defense-doj-trump.html), [WaPo](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/26/justice-dept-charges-james-comey-ex-fbi-director-third-time/)
- 2026-10-09: The E.D.N.C. motions (true threat / First Amendment, and vindictive and selective prosecution) were awaiting decision. The government argues a jury, not the judge, should decide the true-threat question. [gvwire](https://gvwire.com/2026/10/09/the-seashells-case-against-comey-at-a-crossroads/)
- Fourth Circuit (does not count for this question):
  - Wikipedia and other reports put oral argument on September 15, 2026, which conflicts with the "week of November 2" date in the background. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_James_Comey)
  - I found no ruling. A Kalshi market prices reinstatement before 2027 at 7%.

## 4. Base rates
- D.C. grand juries have repeatedly declined to indict in politically charged cases. The reported no-bill for Cassidy Hutchinson is one example. [Time News](https://time.news/grand-jury-declines-to-indict-cassidy-hutchinson/)
- DOJ cases against Trump adversaries have often been dismissed:
  - E.D. Va.: the Comey and Letitia James indictments, November 24, 2025. [Lawfare](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/federal-judge-dismisses-comey-and-james-indictments)
  - D.D.C.: the Floris and Benavides case, November 2, 2026.
- Federal judges dismissing indictments on vindictive-prosecution or true-threat grounds is historically rare. Flanagan's ruling date is unknown and she has kept the case on a 2027 schedule.
- I found no precedent for a "waiverless information" stopping a statute of limitations in this way. McFadden called the issues novel.

## 5. Other forecasts
- Kalshi, "Comey national defense information case (1:26-cr-00229) dismissed": 23% before January 1, 2027; 89% before July 1, 2027.
  - It is unclear whether a superseding indictment under the same case number would count as dismissal for this market.
- Kalshi, "Will James Comey's criminal case be dismissed?": 27% before January 1, 2027; 62% before July 1, 2027.
  - I could not confirm which case this market tracks. It is probably the E.D.N.C. case or the original case.
- Polymarket, "Comey charges dropped by December 31?": 39.5% Yes. The market wording is ambiguous about which case it covers.
- Polymarket, "Comey sentenced to prison in 2026?": 1.15%.
- I found no market that matches "two pending cases on November 13" directly.

## 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- About 2026-11-05: the reported Speedy Trial Act / grand jury deadline in D.D.C.
  - If DOJ gets an indictment under the same case number, that is still one pending case.
  - If it gets one under a new case number while the information is dismissed, there is still one D.C. case pending.
  - A no-bill, or no indictment, could lead to dismissal of the information.
- Any time: McFadden could rule on the limitations motion.
- Any time: Flanagan could rule on the four E.D.N.C. motions.
- Possible: a Fourth Circuit decision. It cannot count as a pending case, but a reinstatement could revive the E.D. Va. district-court case.
- 2026-11-03: Midterm Election Day. DOJ policy discourages overt investigative steps before elections, which could affect when grand jury action happens.

The CBS "30 days" detail and the Speedy Trial Act mechanics are not explained clearly in any source I found. They are worth checking against the docket if you have PACER access.

As of the latest reporting (October 30 to November 2, 2026), Comey still has exactly two pending federal district-court cases: the D.C. information and the North Carolina "seashells" indictment. The main near-term risk is the D.C. case, where November 5 is reportedly the deadline for prosecutors to get a grand jury indictment. I found no report of an indictment, a grand jury refusal ("no bill") or a ruling after October 30.

## 2. Current status

He took it under advisement, did not rule, and left prosecutors free to seek an indictment. The article doesn't give the date, but counting from October 30 it is November 5. The judge also said "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days." [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147)
- 2026-10-30: A DOJ attorney said they had found evidence running to April 2017. ABC says including it could give about six more months to charge. [ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts/story?id=137706147)
- North Carolina case: the four defense motions are fully briefed. I found no ruling from Judge Flanagan, and no oral argument has been scheduled. Comey's next appearance is in January 2027. [Daily Beast](https://www.thedailybeast.com/james-comeys-86-47-trump-seashell-case-gets-even-weirder/), [gvwire/NYT](https://gvwire.com/2026/10/09/the-seashells-case-against-comey-at-a-crossroads/)

- 2026-11-02: In D.C., Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed DOJ's October 20 case against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides for lack of probable cause, calling it "weaponization." This is not Comey's case, but it shows a D.C. court rejecting a similar politically charged prosecution. [HNGN](https://www.hngn.com/articles/273674/20261102/judge-calls-doj-case-against-ex-fbi-officials-weaponization-tosses-it.htm)

It doesn't matter for resolution either way, and I found no decision. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecution_of_James_Comey)

## 4. Base rates
- I found no systematic base rate for this exact situation (a placeholder information filed right at the end of the limitations period, then a race to indict).
- Comparable recent outcomes:
  - 2025: a Virginia grand jury refused to indict Comey on one of the three proposed counts. [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/trumps-newly-appointed-us-attorney-presented-comey-case-grand-jury-sou-rcna233880)
  - 2025-11-24: the Virginia case against Comey was dismissed.
  - 2026-11-02: the Floris/Benavides case was dismissed in D.C.
  - D.C. grand juries have refused to indict in a growing number of cases, which McFadden noted himself.
- North Carolina: Flanagan has had ripe motions since about late September with no ruling for over a month. That suggests a ruling within the next 10 days is possible but not signaled.

## 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- Around 2026-11-05: the reported deadline for a D.C. grand jury indictment. Possible outcomes:

forecasts.reasoning:
**(a) Time left and what Yes requires.** About 10 days remain (to 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026). Yes requires both of these to hold on that date:
- **D.C.:** a charging document naming Comey must still be pending in D.C. That can be the October 5 information, an indictment in the same case, or an indictment under a new D.C. case number.
- **E.D.N.C.:** the seashells indictment must not have been dismissed.

**(b) Status quo.** Both cases are pending today, so the status quo is Yes. The one built-in threat is the reported November 5 Speedy Trial Act deadline for a D.C. indictment.

**(c) Base rate.** Federal criminal cases are rarely dismissed in any given 10-day window, perhaps under 5%. This D.C. case is different because it has a hard deadline and an unusual charging device that may not stop the limitations clock. Among politically charged D.C. matters in 2025-26, grand juries have no-billed or courts have tossed cases fairly often, roughly a third to half the time. Combining these, I start around 70-80% Yes.

**(d) Strongest evidence.**
- **For Yes:**
  - Both cases were pending as of November 2-3, with no dismissal, no-bill or adverse ruling reported.
  - On October 30, DOJ said it is "diligently" going to the grand jury and cited new evidence of overt acts as late as April 2017, which would give it a later limitations window.
  - On October 30, McFadden took the motion under advisement rather than dismissing.
  - Flanagan has kept E.D.N.C. on a 2027 schedule, set no oral argument and left the motions undecided since late September.
  - Kalshi prices the D.C. case dismissal before January 1, 2027 at only 23%.
- **For No:**
  - November 5 is the reported last day for an indictment.
  - McFadden was openly skeptical on October 30 ("ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days").
  - D.C. grand juries have refused to indict in politically charged cases, such as the reported Hutchinson no-bill.
  - On November 2, a magistrate dismissed the Floris and Benavides case for lack of probable cause, calling it "weaponization."
  - Election Day (November 3) and DOJ pre-election norms may squeeze the time left for grand jury action.

**(e) Scenarios.**
- **No:** The grand jury no-bills, or DOJ cannot present the case in time. Comey moves to dismiss after November 5, and McFadden dismisses the information around November 9-12. Only E.D.N.C. remains.
- **Yes:** A D.C. grand jury returns an indictment, in the same case or a new one, by November 5. Alternatively, McFadden simply has not ruled by November 13. Flanagan stays silent, and two cases are pending.

**(f) From base rate to final number.**
- **D.C.:** I put the chance of no indictment by November 5 at about 35%. Given that, I put the chance of dismissal entered by November 13 at about 60%. A small extra risk comes from a limitations ruling with no replacement charge. That leaves the D.C. case pending with roughly 77% probability.
- **E.D.N.C.:** I put the chance of a dismissal ruling within 10 days at about 6%, so roughly 94% that it stays pending.
- **Combined:** 0.77 × 0.94 ≈ 72%. The Kalshi pricing implies slightly lower D.C. dismissal risk in the short term, so I nudge up to 73%.

Probability: 73%

**(a) Time left and what is needed for Yes.** There are about 10 days until 23:59 UTC on November 13, 2026. Yes requires that on that date at least two federal district-court criminal cases naming Comey are still pending. In practice that means:
- the D.D.C. case (the information, or a replacement or superseding indictment) has not been dismissed in full, and
- the E.D.N.C. seashells indictment has not been dismissed.

A new D.C. indictment under a different case number would also count.

**(b) Status quo.** As of November 3, two cases are pending and neither has been dismissed. If nothing changes, the answer is Yes.

**(c) Base rate.** Federal criminal cases are rarely dismissed in any particular 10-day window. Even with pending dispositive motions, the chance per case is usually well under 10%. Two cases both surviving 10 days would normally resolve Yes about 90% or more of the time. The D.C. case is unusual because of the reported November 5 Speedy Trial Act / indictment deadline, so that base rate needs adjusting.

**(d) Strongest evidence.**
- **For Yes:**
  - On October 30, McFadden took the motion under advisement rather than dismissing, and signaled he would wait for DOJ's grand jury effort.
  - DOJ says it is "diligently" pursuing a D.C. indictment, has new evidence, and has possible overt acts through April 2017. That would extend the limitations window, and a superseding indictment in the same case keeps it pending.
  - Flanagan has kept the E.D.N.C. case on a 2027 schedule, with no ruling as of late October and no hearing set.
  - Kalshi prices dismissal of the D.C. case before January 1, 2027 at only 23%. That covers a much longer window than ours, and it would count some outcomes as "dismissal" that leave a D.C. case pending here.
- **For No:**
  - ABC reports November 5 as the last day to indict before the information is dismissed.
  - McFadden was skeptical ("ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days").
  - D.C. grand juries have returned no-bills in politically charged cases.
  - On November 2 a D.D.C. magistrate judge tossed the Floris/Benavides case as "weaponization."
  - Flanagan's motions have been ripe since September and she could rule on the papers at any time.

**(e) Scenarios.**
- **No:** DOJ cannot get a D.C. indictment by November 5, or gets a no-bill. Comey moves immediately, and McFadden enters an order dismissing the information around November 10. Alternatively, Flanagan grants the First Amendment / true-threat motion in the next week.
- **Yes:** DOJ obtains a D.C. indictment, either superseding in the same case or under a new number, or McFadden simply has not ruled by November 13. Meanwhile Flanagan stays silent or denies the motions.

**(f) From base rate to final probability.** I start from about 90% (status quo, short window). For the D.C. case, I estimate roughly a 45-50% chance of no indictment by the deadline, and roughly a 35-45% chance that McFadden actually enters a dismissal by November 13 in that case. That is about 15-18% risk, in line with the Kalshi 23% over the longer window. I add about 5% risk from a Flanagan dismissal in the 10-day window. That leaves combined No risk of about 20%. I moved down from 90% to about 80%, mainly because of the concrete November 5 deadline and the hostile signals from the D.C. bench.

Probability: 79%

(a) The outcome is known on November 13, 2026, about 10 days away. For Yes, at least two federal district-court criminal cases naming Comey must be pending at 23:59 UTC that day. In practice that means:
- the E.D.N.C. seashells case is not dismissed, and
- the D.D.C. case survives, either because the information is not dismissed, or because a replacement indictment is pending under the same or a new case number.

(b) The status quo is Yes. Exactly two cases are pending now, and nothing has been dismissed as of November 3.

(c) Base rate: federal criminal cases rarely get fully disposed of within an arbitrary 10-day window, probably under 5% per case. The D.D.C. case is not typical, though. It faces an imminent deadline (reported as November 5), a skeptical judge and D.C. grand juries that have recently refused to indict. A fair starting point is about 85% that two cases stay pending.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:**
  - On October 30, McFadden declined to rule and appeared to be waiting for an indictment.
  - DOJ says it is going to the grand jury "very diligently." It has new evidence of overt acts through April 2017, which gives it room to charge outside the October 2016 limitations problem.
  - Judge Flanagan has kept the E.D.N.C. case on a 2027 schedule, with no oral argument set (October 9 reporting).
  - Kalshi prices dismissal of the D.C. case before January 1, 2027 at only 23%. That market likely also counts a dismissal paired with a replacement indictment.
- **For No:**
  - ABC reports November 5 as the Speedy Trial Act deadline.
  - D.C. grand juries have returned no-bills in politically charged cases, such as the reported Hutchinson no-bill.
  - McFadden was skeptical of the waiverless information and called a no-bill an "exercise in futility."
  - Magistrate Judge Faruqui threw out the Floris and Benavides case on November 2 as "weaponization."
